[27:42] field labour for three years, which labour was  of more value than the cost of a [new] slave.”

[27:54] Africans and indentured servants worked  side-by-side on the slave plantations. 
[28:00] And this process was followed by the other  colonizers as well. The Portuguese, French,  
[28:05] British, and Dutch started out with serfs,  then needed indentured servants to work the  
[28:10] plantations, and then began buying slaves. While  they all got there in a slightly different way,  
[28:16] this process of Spain that I have described would  repeat itself with almost every American colony  
[28:22] until the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade ended. There was always some resistance to the harsh  
[28:30] treatment of enslaved Afrians, but it was very  limited. For example, Spain and Portugal passed  
[28:36] laws limiting the amount of slaves you could carry  on a ship, how much food they should receive,  
[28:42] and a rest day on sundays. But these rules were  easily circumvented. Instead of slaves you would  
[28:49] just have more “crew”... who you then sold off  in the colonies. And if someone checked if your  
[28:56] slaves were treated well, you could just bribe  them. And anyone who actually obeyed the law was  
[29:04] easily outcompeted by another slave plantation  owner who did not. And a common smuggling tactic  
[29:12] was to bring your slaves to the Atlantic  Ocean, then find someone to “attack” you,  
[29:19] they then “steal” your slaves from you, and  in the process they were so clumsy that they  
[29:27] accidentally dropped a bag of silver. A bag  of silver roughly equal to the cost of those  
[29:33] slaves… What a coincidence… And when you arrive in  the Americas you’re no longer breaking any laws. 
[29:44] Chapter 7: The Triangular Trade Up until this point all trade with the  
[29:51] Americas went through Europe. None of the slaves  traveled from Africa to the Americas directly. But  
[29:57] this began to change with Congo. Because Congo  and the Americas have a special relationship. 
[30:04] Look at this map. It shows wind patterns from  across the world. There are 2 wind patterns  
[30:09] going from Africa to the Americas. One is up here  going from Northwest Africa and another from down  
[30:15] here next to Congo. The winds could take a ship  from Congo directly to Northern Brazil. And all  
[30:22] of a sudden it was possible to cut out Spain and  Portugal and trade directly with the American  
[30:28] slave owners. This route was first discovered in  the 1520s and it revolutionized the Trans-Atlantic  
[30:35] trade. And from the on the Trans-Atlantic  Slave Trade became the Triangular Trade. 
[30:42] The way the Triangular Trade worked is that a  ship would be built in Europe. There they would  
[30:47] buy European manufactured goods such as guns,  steel, and wool. They would then sail south,  
[30:53] sell their goods, and buy slaves. Then they’d  sail directly to the Americas where they’d  
[30:59] sell the slaves and buy sugar cane. Then they  came back to Europe where they would sell the  
[31:03] sugar cane to buy more manufactured goods  to start the whole journey all over again. 
[31:09] And Congo was very happy with this change.  Because Congo was much further away from Europe  
[31:15] and therefore never joined the Trans-Saharan  Slave Trade. Now all of a sudden they could  
[31:20] join the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade. Within  10 years they had already sold 5k slaves,  
[31:27] Portugal established embassies, and Congo  converted to Christianity.[HALLELUJAH] Because  
[31:35] as explained earlier: It was okay for Christians  to enslave people of other faiths. Which meant  
[31:41] that as the only Chrisitan country in the region,  they could enslave everybody around them. The way  
[31:47] they saw it was that the other Africans were  foreigners. And they could earn a lot of money  
[31:52] selling one foreigner to another foreigner. And  so Congo slowly became a military state constantly  
[31:59] at war with everybody around them in order to get  more slaves to sell to the Portuguese. And as the  
[32:05] American colonies grew, so did their demand for  slaves. And as the demand for slaves increased,  
[32:11] so did the amount of wars Congo fought. All the  way up to the 19th century Congo would become a  
[32:16] battlezone in order to earn money selling  slaves to work in the sugar plantations. 
[32:22] But the Native Americans were dying so quickly  that the Spanish colonies needed A LOT more  
[32:29] slaves than Portugal could sell. And so in  the 1530 Spain would set up their own slave  
[32:35] trade and they created a monopoly to control this  trade. Meaning that only the people who held this  
[32:41] monopoly were allowed to trade slaves. And because  the Spanish colonies always needed more slaves,  
[32:46] the trade was very profitable, and a lot of people  tried buying the Spanish slave monopoly. In fact,  
[32:53] it became a geopolitical objective for various  countries to get this monopoly. Because if your  
[33:00] country held the monopoly, your country would get  rich. And so the monopoly became a tool by which  
[33:06] Spain could assure other countries’ cooperation  or else the monopoly would go to someone else. 
[33:13] In the meantime Portugal had created their own  slave plantations. But they were earning a lot  
[33:18] of money off of the slave trade and so decided  to stick with Native Americans slaves in their  
[33:27] own colonies. In the 1560s 2 epidemics killed most  of the Native Americans in Brazil and in the 1570s  
[33:35] Portugal also switched to enslaved Africans.  By 1600 Portugal and Spain both had colonies  
[33:42] full of slave plantations producing sugar.  Between 1576-1591 alone Portugal bought nearly  
[33:49] 50k slaves… That’s over 3k per year on average. And then the Portuguese Empire and the Spanish  
[33:59] Empire were merged into one single empire. In  1580 the king of Portugal died and the king  
[34:06] of Spain inherited Portugal, because  they were cousins. And at this point  
[34:16] Spain completely controlled the Trans-Atlantic  Slave Trade. They controlled the supply of  
[34:21] slaves and they controlled the sugar plantations. But this leaves us with 1 very important question:  
[34:29] why was sugar of all things the reason for the  Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, for all the slave  
[34:34] wars in West Africa, and for European kings to  change their foreign policy over? Well the reason  
[34:40] for this is that Europeans in the 16th century  started getting richer: they had better tools,  
[34:46] created basic machinery, and discovered more  efficient ways of growing food. All this meant  
[34:52] they had a bit more money. And according to UN  statistics, when poor people stop being poor one  
[34:57] of the first things they will buy is sugar. The  reason for this is that a poor person is never  
[35:02] getting enough calories per day because they  don’t have enough money…. Sugar has a lot of  
[35:08] calories. So adding sugar to your food means you  have more energy in life. And this is why Spain  
[35:14] never had enough slaves: Europeans were getting  richer, meaning they wanted to buy more sugar,  
[35:20] meaning Spain had to build more plantations,  meaning they had to buy more slaves. 
[35:28] Chapter 8: Competition. The first danger to Spanish dominance  
[35:35] were the Dutch… The Dutch Republic used to be part  of the Spanish Empire. And as a result they joined  
[35:41] the Trans-Altnatic Slave Trade as soon as Spain  did, refining sugar, and selling it to the rest  
[35:46] of Europe. But a century later in 1579 the Dutch  Republic declared independence and fought the 80  
[35:53] Years War with Spain. All of a sudden the Dutch  could no longer buy sugar cane from the Spanish.  
[35:59] And this meant that the Dutch would have to make  their own sugar cane. Afterall, they already had  
[36:04] experience from their time in the Spanish Empire.  So they began setting up sugar plantations in  
[36:09] modern day Brazil and over time conquered most of  the colonies in North-Eastern South America. And  
[36:15] just as the Spanish and Portuguese, they started  out with Native American workers, then indentured  
[36:21] servants, and lastly enslaved Africans. The Dutch Republic financed all this with  
[36:26] money from the middle class. They created a  shareholder system whereby you could own a  
[36:30] share in a particular enterprise. So for example,  instead of 10 people each owning 1 ship, 10 people  
[36:38] would each own 10% of 10 ships. Because if you own  1 ship and that ship sinks then you lose all your  
[36:46] money. If you own 10% of a ship and that ship  sinks then you still have most of your money. 
[36:53] The Dutch created national companies to handle  all their long-distance trading. And in the case  
[36:58] of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, the Dutch  created the Dutch West India Comapny in 1621.  
[37:04] This company would hold the monopoly on all  trade with the American colonies. From now on  
[37:09] you couldn’t just buy a license to trade,  you had to join the company as one of its  
[37:13] traders. But the company opposed the slave trade.  Because from the Dutch perspective at the time,  
[37:19] a country became rich if they could do more  trade. In order to trade you need to have  
[37:24] people with money. So you want to create a strong  middle class full of customer. But a slave has no  
[37:30] money. So for every person you enslave you lose  a potential customer. And so the Dutch West India  
[37:36] Company opposed the slave trade… for now. Btw,  this is the basis of early capitalist philosophy. 
[37:43] The Dutch West India Company was allowed to  have their own army and navy. Because it was  
[37:48] simply more efficient to have a company handle  their own military than for the government to  
[37:53] protect trade ships. And so the company went  to war in the Americas to conquer some more  
[37:57] colonies. And in many cases they freed the slave,  gave them weapons, and sent them to fight their  
[38:03] former masters. But as the Dutch conquered  more slave plantations and slave markets,

[38:53] Shortly after the Dutch, French joined  the slave trade as well. The started by

[44:16] Chapter 10: The Rise And  Fall of National Companies

[45:01] France and England wanted to do the same.  And they combined their own Trans-Atlantic

[47:53] MANY slaves that the English simply couldn’t  produce enough of these products to buy the

[50:22] The Spanish did not have a national company, but  still faced the same competition. Their inability

[52:09] enough money in the British economy to buy  all the shares of the company. Then the price
